subject: botany_2
question_text: Can a disease be detected before its symptoms appear? Explain the principle involved.

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.46, printed question 119. Revised 2026-09-05: s1_yes's why said both techniques detect the pathogen rather than the body's reaction, which is false for ELISA — NCERT states infection is detected by the pathogen's antigens or by the antibodies made against it — so the why now states each principle separately.

insider_note: Yes, then two techniques with their two principles. Four facts in four lines.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The two techniques
lines: YES. A disease can be detected before its symptoms
steps.why: PCR copies the pathogen's own nucleic acid until even a very small amount can be detected, and ELISA detects the pathogen's antigen or the antibody made against it. Both can give a result before any symptom appears.
common_mistakes: Answering with a bare yes. The techniques are half the mark.
Naming only one technique. Both PCR and ELISA are expected.
steps.memory_tip: Detect the pathogen, not the symptom.

steps.label: Their principles
steps.margin_note: Both principles named, one line of explanation each.

lines.text: PCR amplifies the gene; ELISA binds antigen

lines: The principle of PCR is GENE AMPLIFICATION:
even a very small amount of pathogen DNA is copied
The principle of ELISA is ANTIGEN-ANTIBODY
INTERACTION: the pathogen's antigen binds a
steps.why: A tiny amount of pathogen is invisible until it is either multiplied or made to bind something detectable, which is exactly what the two techniques do.
common_mistakes: Swapping the principles. PCR is amplification; ELISA is antigen-antibody.
Giving the names with no principles. The question asks for the PRINCIPLE.
steps.memory_tip: One multiplies the evidence; the other makes it stick to something.
